doc.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 5, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Sextet choice, writing intros and endings, telethons, Basie and Eartha Kitt
summary: Gibbs insisted on a sextet (Colin Bailey, Monty Budwig, Mike Melvoin, Herb Ellis), explains his intro-and-ending arranging trick and telethon system, and tells of Basie, Getz and Eartha Kitt on the show.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: they said, “Okay we want you, it’s your job, but Steve Allen had a nine piece orchestra, we’ll give you a nine piece orchestra.” I said, “I don’t want it.” They said, “Well what do you mean?” I said, “You mean they give me a big band because we’re opposite Johnny Carson? Or opposite Elliot Lawrence who was with Les Crane — those shows at that time they all had 16 piece bands. And to me a 16 piece band — give me a sextet. I said sextet? Can you make it with a sextet? You see working with Steve Allen, of course I didn’t know who was or what kind of talent he would have, but say he’d get Sarah Vaughan on the show or whatever. What’s the most important thing? A rhythm section. A rhythm section. That’s the whole thing. They traveled with a rhythm section. So I hired the best rhythm section I could find: Colin Bailey was a monster drummer, Monty Budwig who was a monster bass player, Mike Melvoin a monster piano player, and Herb Ellis. And I hired a guy who played all the reeds. And when the scenes would come and if they had a big orchestra arrangement at rehearsal we would just play down the song, you know. And what I would do I would take and arrange — everybody went to lunch and I would take that arrangement and use like their introduction, but not use their introduction, I’d write my own introduction for that song and I’d write my own ending. And in between I’d say okay here the flute will play the high, will play 16 bars, or Herb Ellis will play this. You know. And slowly I learned something years ago, you give them an opening they can understand and give them a closing they understand, that’s all people will remember. Of which I will go into something — a wild story using that theme. I was conducting a lot of telethons in those days. In the old days it wasn’t like a Jerry Lewis Telethon where they rehearse all week and they already had 80 million dollars that the corporations gave them. People were on stage collecting money. And here in California I had my own band. But we got — Steve Allen got called to do a telethon in New York. So I flew in with him, I took Frank Capp on drums, my drummer, and Paul Smith who was doing my TV shows. Paul Smith is the monster of all television piano players. And I called my friend Al Epstein, to give me a band in New York, a real great band with great musicians you know. And so what kind of talent do you get in New York City? You get all the Broadway shows and you never get the star, you always get one of the people in the show, and they never sing the main title of the song. They sing some obscure — which I never heard before, and there’s no rehearsal and they just throw it immediately at you. You kept the music from the Broadway show and you look at it, everything is marked up. You go from G to F and A to B, go back to R, go home and have a glass of water and come back. It’s so ridiculous nobody said — so I found a system. I said, “Here’s what we are going to do. Play the introduction, right? Because that’s written, no problem. Play the introduction, Paul Smith, and I think it was Paul West, the bass player in New York, and Frank Capp. You guys will accompany the singer and everybody come

in at Letter D, the ending.” Play the intro — the singer never knew we never played the middle. We’d never do it. So that’s what I learned. So I did that for my TV shows, and then, you know it was, it just came naturally to me because the harder part got later on. See all the talent we had for the first maybe two or three weeks, and that’s why Regis, in last, where all the talent that already were booked for Steve Allen. And Steve was a big jazz fan so he’d have Sarah Vaughan, Stan Getz, Oscar Peterson, Count Basie. And Regis was never hip to that. You know he didn’t know these people — so I remember one time when we — cause I was like second banana, it was like Count Basie and the band, on the show. And they’re in the middle of the floor, and Regis interviewing him and Count Basie can yes and no ya to death. You ask him a question, “Yes.” “No” and now after about three, four, five yes and nos, Regis is going in the toilet. I said, “Regis, let me ask Basie a question.” “Yeah, come on down, Terry.” Now I did a two month tour with Basie plus I worked opposite him many times at Birdland. I said, “Hey Basie, tell them the time, the story where Sarah Vaughan” — now whatever it is, now he had to tell the story. So Regis loved me for that, see? Same thing happened with Stan Getz he’d yes and no ya to death. So he had me close with the jazz. But after the two or three weeks of the jazz then people like Eartha Kitt and people that Regis had more in common with came on the show. And Eartha Kitt was wild, I’ll tell you, that’s a wild story. I’m not sure if I wrote about it. But Eartha used to come into Birdland when I used to work opposite Basie and Sarah Vaughan. And I was only the baby. It was always Count Basie, Sarah Vaughn, Terry Gibbs; Duke Ellington, Dinah Washington, Terry Gibbs. So she knew me as the kid at the club. Now here I’m a musical director. She came in with the music for an 84 piece orchestra with violins and everything. And I told Regis, I’m not going to say — I said, “Eartha, do me a favor. Let me do something, let me do something when everybody goes out to lunch, just sit and talk to Regis, and we’ll get a chance to rehearse before the show. We’ll get a chance, and I’ll tell you what I’m doing. And so what I did, I had Herb Ellis, who was the greatest accompanist in the world, play rubato — no tempo. Because Eartha Kitt could sneak around. In fact I wrote a song called “Earthanova” for when she used to come on the show a lot, it was a bossa nova. And she would walk in and slink in, like you know that sound? And so I had that and then I’d have, if we went in tempo I did one here we played in tempo with the rhythm section. And she could sing. And she loved me for that. She really loved me for that. So now I became not a little kid anymore, I became the musical director of the Regis show. But I would do that with a lot of acts that would come in. I learned how to do that with the dream band I had with Steve Allen with the big band, of course it was big. When I had a little band — everything was jazz with Steve Allen you know.
